cands.name: Amanda Marie Green
cands.bio: Democratic nominee for the open 2nd district seat. Spent a decade as an operations director and pricing expert on U.S. government contracts, including work with the largest implementing partner for USAID. Studied at Florida State University. Won a four-way primary with 33.4%. Has never held elected office.
cands.local_ties: Born at the Naval Hospital in San Diego, moved to Florida at age two, raised mainly in St. Petersburg; now lives near Tallahassee in the Big Bend with her husband and infant son.

record.text: Campaign priorities: rural development and cost of living (groceries, health care, housing, gas); says she would seek a seat on the Agriculture Committee (WTXL).
Won the Aug 18, 2026 Democratic primary with 33.4% (20,705 votes) over Yen Bailey, Brice Barnes and Nicholas Zateslo (Becker analysis).

endorsements.text: Florida AFL-CIO; Leon County Sheriff Walt McNeil; former U.S. Rep. Allen Boyd; former state Sen. Daryl Jones; after the primary, former U.S. Rep. Al Lawson and state Reps. Gallop Franklin and Allison Tant (per Wikipedia 2026 district page citing Florida Politics/AOL; Florida Politics pages are paywalled and were not opened).

cands.gaps: Wikipedia calls her an 'operations manager'; her own site says operations director and pricing expert (used the latter). No fundraising or outside-money details verified. Not to be confused with the playwright of the same name.

cands.name: Austin Rogers
cands.bio: Republican nominee for the open 2nd district seat (Rep. Neal Dunn is retiring). Attorney and former general counsel to U.S. Sen. Rick Scott. Won an eight-way August primary with 30.5%. Has never held elected office. Campaign themes: border security, business, military and law enforcement, AI and children's online safety.
cands.local_ties: Panama City native; says he was 'raised right here in the 2nd District.' Residency and voter-registration timing were challenged by primary rivals (see controversies).

record.text: As Sen. Rick Scott's general counsel he handled legislative and oversight work (including Eastern Shipbuilding matters and aid for local fishermen and small businesses, per his campaign launch coverage).
Says he drafted a bill on Chinese surrogacy that he wants to advance nationally as the Safe Kids Act (WFSU, Aug 18, 2026).

money_notes.text: Raised about $725,000 in roughly two months after filing Jan 29, 2026, including $350,000 of his own money (Floridian Press, April 2026).
Outside group Panhandle Patriots reported a first-quarter filing totaling $2 million in support of Rogers (Floridian Press, April 2026).

controversies.text: In the May 2026 GOP debate, rival Jim Norton questioned Rogers's Florida residency; Rogers pushed back (WFSU, May 19, 2026).

Aug 13-14, 2026 primary attack ads by a new committee, Freedom Against Federal Overreach, said Rogers 'wasn't even registered to vote in Florida until March 17th,' lived in an Airbnb, and that his former employer did business with China. The ads were sponsored by a rival-aligned group; no response from Rogers was reported in the article.

endorsements.text: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, plus Reps. Tom Emmer, Jim Jordan, Guy Reschenthaler and Greg Steube; state Sen. Jay Trumbull; mayors of Panama City Beach, Graceville and Lynn Haven; retired Lt. Gen. Darryl Roberson (per Wikipedia 2026 district page citing Florida Politics/Washington Reporter; those pages were not opened). Trump did not endorse him in the primary (Voz).

cands.gaps: No verified campaign website or social accounts (rogersforcongress.com looked like a placeholder). Education (a source lists Duke law degree) unverified so omitted. No photo used: the only portrait found (WFSU) is a family photo with young children. Date he moved to Florida not established. Ballotpedia blocked automated fetches.
